title: Stop Scapegoating Screens Try Doing Something That Actually Helps Young People November 9, 2026
author: Stefan Bauschard
source: Education Disrupted: Teaching and Learning in An AI World (stefanbauschard.substack.com),
summary: Stefan Bauschard argues that blaming screens for young people's problems is a convenient distraction from the more important question of what schools should teach in an age of AI. He accepts that excessive screen time can harm students, but notes that many things in schooling can be harmful in excess, from heavy homework to passive lecturing, and that phone bans and traditional instruction let schools avoid rethinking curriculum, assessment and purpose. Citing a 2026 national study in which lockable phone pouches cut phone use but barely moved test scores, he says screen time measures exposure to a medium, not educational value. He points to weak early-career outcomes, including high underemployment among recent graduates and a Stanford finding of lower employment among young workers in AI-exposed jobs. He contends that educators who preach grit and adaptability should show those qualities by questioning their own assumptions and experimenting with new models of learning.
points: Screen time measures exposure to a medium, not educational value, so a screen-free worksheet that an AI can complete in seconds is no more valuable than mindless scrolling.
Phone bans and traditional instruction are attractive because they let schools avoid changing curriculum, instruction and assessment, which is the real conversation AI demands.
A 2026 national study found lockable phone pouches reduced phone use but produced little overall improvement in test scores, with modest gains for some groups and over time for well-being.

Entry-level job data, including recent-graduate underemployment and weaker employment for young workers in AI-exposed fields, challenge the assumption that the standard school-to-college pathway delivers.
Educators who ask students to show grit, creativity and risk-taking should demonstrate them by reconsidering their own institutions, assessments and purposes.
quotes: There is something remarkably convenient about blaming screens for the problems facing young people today.
We seem remarkably concerned about the potential harms of excessive screen time, but far less interested in the potential harms of excessive traditional schooling.
Screen time is a measure of exposure to a medium. It is not a measure of educational value.
We should evaluate educational practices by what students actually gain from them, not by how closely they resemble our memories of school.
We have confused the historical value of our curriculum with its continued adequacy for preparing students for the future.
We’re trying to protect traditional assessments from AI rather than asking whether those assessments still make sense.
You cannot credibly preach adaptability to young people while treating your own institution as too sacred to change.
